content:
Hi there, I am working on a Lean (v4.29.0) project on my M3 MacBook Pro. When I run lake build the build is taking a very long time (multiple minutes for small files). It appears that the lean process is running on the efficiency cores of the CPU and I am seeing only ~10% CPU usage per process.

Any ideas on what could be causing this?
This is unfortunately not concrete enough for us to help you. Could you provide at least an example project or even better a #mwe if possible.

@Henrik Böving I think I tracked down issue myself. The culprit seems to be importing the entirety of Mathlib at the root of my project, causing each file to spend time loading the Mathlib files instead of compiling. The build got a lot faster when I switched to only importing that parts that I need. However, the old version was still a lot faster on my Linux machine than on my Mac, which seems strange.

We have observed behavior of non Linux devices taking a lot longer to access a large import closure before. Does your Mac have some sort of cyber security software that might be monitoring file access?
Actually that could be the case as this is my work computer, which has, e.g., Microsoft Defender on it.

So Microsoft defender was precisely the culprit when my new fast Mac was taking a huge amount of time on lean files. I could lake build on the command line and it be slow the first time, then immediate, then five minutes later slow again (after no changes). I fixed it by disabling Defender scanning on my home directory.
I will add it to my Defender exclusions as well, thanks!

I doubt it's the Tahoe OS that makes this very slow. Claude says sys takes 94% but on linux sys is < 10%.

Lean is written in a style that spaws many process which I believe causes a significant change from linux to others.

Even on Linux, it suffers from consuming too much memory for my own use case because of too many processes.

I'm actually rewriting lean compiler in Rust just so I can have a much faster iteration for development.
I saw many other lagness of software on MacOS Tahoe. I strongly suspect this is OS-related issue. Maybe something Tahoe that makes dylib related stuff or fork+exec stuff slow.
I might have fixed the issues by basically disabling all safety checks of MacOS.
I feel like MacOS is overly cautious.
Wait, still doesn't work. Maybe lean compiler is just not for MacOS.

I think that rather than posting a vague stream of consciousness it might be more helpful to have an explicit description of a problem you're having. Many people here are using lean on MacOS no problem.
I'm still in the process of debugging this.

I'm running a very large lean build. Comparable to mathlib itself. So it's probably not very typical.

The problem is just it's being very slow. Spending way more time in the system space.

As I'm not using lean in vscode, but rather building things from scratch, so can be a totally different experience.
And I'm not exactly expecting lean compiler to just work amazingly on every platform in every possible case because it would mean too much.
Maybe for my case to work, would require a fundamental redesign of the lean compiler, which I would rather do it myself than asking the community.

I'm using Lean as transpilation target my provers. This is different use case than most people. So it doesn't surprise me it unveils problems not heard of by others. But I don't feel Lean has the obligation to do good for all cases. The bootstrap of lean compiler is quite convoluted. I'm just in the process of rewriting.

So two things:

1) We generally discourage people posting "stream of consciousness" messages on this Zulip (you just posted 5 messages in a row). Maybe, if you have something to say, just post one message?

2) Your posts are, as far as I can see, simply far too vague for anyone to help you. If you are able to post some explicit problem, some debugging output, a link to the build or the thing you're trying to compile etc etc, then perhaps someone can help you. But simply saying "Maybe for my case to work, would require a fundamental redesign of the lean compiler" is what seems to me to be a (currently) completely unjustified claim, and all this does is makes people (incorrectly) think that Lean is broken in some way on MacOS, which is definitively not the case as far as I am concerned at least.

In short, your constant stream of "I am doing something complicated and I think Lean is broken" posts are not achieving anything at all other than making noise on this Zulip and spreading dubious information.

Maybe you want to either consider posting a concrete example of a problem you are having, or working on your problem offline rather than giving us these "updates" which give the community no concrete and actionable information about the problems you are having.
Then I just won't speak then. Feel like this is the wrong place for me to talk.

It's the wrong place to post unstructured vague thoughts of the form "I am stuck and it doesn't work". This Zulip is the right place for precise questions, containing concrete examples which other people can run so that they can experience the same problems which you have. It is not a chat room, it is a professional research forum.

Ok, let me try be precise, see if this woks:

I'm building a new prover that transpiles to lean. Unfortunately the transpilation is very very large.

Building the transpiled lean code on MacOS turns out to be at least 10times slower than Linux, which forces me to use linux for development.

Unfortunately I can't provide an example because I develop that in private.

And this is not my thread also. I'm just adding input to the original poster.

I'm interested in this degradation of behavior from linux to MacOs and interested in what's causing it. And the figuring out process of that takes quite a while. I didn't reach a valuable conclusion to contribute.

I'm not observing rustc etc. to have any similar degration even for very large projects.

Is this accurate and precise enough? Sorry I can't provide the code.

And I'm not a user that asks for help about using lean. I'm mainly about creating better and better provers. I'm interested in design philosophy rather than debating which community is the best. I'm seeing interesting design of lean that makes it better than isa and rocq in many aspects. Still, I'm eagerly poking to see where it fails.

Kevin seems to be in the mindset that I'm trying decredit lean. This is clearly not my intention. I'm using lean for a purpose it's not designed for and it's very normal in the programming language design world that we are finding defects of one tool used in one area not best fitting for it and to think of better plan. And I'm basically 30% towards rewrite lean prover in rust out of curiosity. Although I have no interests to make it public.

The rule is strict though, lol. I can respect that totally. Not everyone is a frequent user of zulip. I literally have little idea what to say properly. I'll just stop saying things here.

And there is one important I want to point:

the attempt to rewrite XXX project in another language is not hard and can be helpful to show future directions.

The Bun author in Anthropic is rewriting Bun from Zig to Rust, just to see what's going on.

As AI coding is strong, it's totally not surprising to rewrite a new compiler in matters of weeks.

I totally understand Kevin's confusion, as the community seems to be mostly Lean users rather than nerds like me who are interested in writing new compilers or provers.

But it's really not the case that:

  1. writing provers informally for exploring ideas is unthinkable (quite easy now if experienced, I've been doing system language design for 4 years and provers for 2 years, written tons of code before, not that good, but enough to guide AI to have some slop done)
  2. I meant to build a better lean. What I really want to see from rewriting lean compiler is to have a useful comparison. The current Lean compiler form is too hard for me to study. In Rust form, I can freely poke around and see what's causing the issue.

In the world of normal programming, we have tons of different languages, from high level to low level, python, C, Cpp, Assembly, Zig. It's a sign of prosperity rather than division. No one will normally think lean has to perfectly fit into every single aspect for theorem proving. In fact, I'm thinking of a design similar to metamath by Mario that can play as the LLVM of the theorem proving world.

As I mainly spent times in a different world (the world of vibe coders) than contributing to Mathlib, it's natural that I speak from a different angle than people in here. And previously I've found out it's a bit awkward to communicate with Lean users. I'll just save my talking here to avoid troubles like this, because it really takes time to spit out this much to make things clear.

If anyone is interested in new prover design, let's chat in private. I'm currently working on something. But I have zero intention to cause troubles in the Lean community which arguably contributed so much to the world of theorem proving.

And I basically was so vague is because my issue is very likely too hard to be helped directly.

It's nearly impossible to reduce to a minimal not working example, as the problem only occurs at scale.

This is very likely my own misuse of Lean which accidently is a problem in MacOS but somehow mitigated in Linux.

I've faced this before.

It took me about 2months to figure it out. Oh, I didn't give lean compiler enough type arguments for it to infer type classes quickly. It's really hard because mathlib is a big system and my project is really really messy.

So my intention was, "my case is so messy, I don't want to waste people's time".

While I sympathize with you if you're running into a frustrating issue, no, in the software community it's still not considered precise to say you're having a performance problem (or any issue) and to not share a specific piece of code to reproduce it, regardless of whether you're developing something in private. Usually either that means you get to make it not private anymore, or that the work becomes on you to create a minimal reproducer of the problem which you can share, which you may need to do anyways to get someone to look at it.

Essentially you provided other surrounding detail, but not anything useful for actually diagnosing whatever issue you're running into.

Again though I think it's understandable to be frustrated, and cross-platform issues are particularly frustrating, but as-is, what you've provided I think has zero chance of someone being able to help.

I'm not asking for help here. I would say it clearly if I REALLY WANTED TO GET YOUR HELP.
THIS IS NOT MY POST. Next time, I'll just make it short or don't say anything.
I feel like many here are focusing on what's the right way to talk too much. In other places, Zulip is relatively casual. Github is the way to put serious effort. Well, it just seems to me that this community is too serious on things for me. I'll learn to respect it.

I'm still waiting for more info from original poster. I'm curious to know if the original poster has solved his/her issue. I think we are causing unnecessary noise for the original post. If anyone want to teach me a lesson in how to talk in zulip, just send me private chat. Let's stop polluting this thread.

I'm turning this thread off. Everyone is busy, don't waste on me.
